performers: Skidmore College Orchestra; cellist and conductor uncredited
intro: The finale of Elgar’s Cello Concerto in E minor, Op. 85 (Allegro — Moderato — Allegro ma non troppo) opens at a vigorous pace until the cello breaks it off. Near the end, themes from the Adagio and from the concerto’s opening return before a brief, fast close.

sections.label: Intro · Orchestra, then cello recitative
sections.mNote: A brisk orchestral flourish, then the cello’s recitative

sections.label: A · March theme, cello, Allegro ma non troppo
sections.mNote: Allegro ma non troppo, marked risoluto.

sections.label: B · Cello and orchestra alternate phrases
sections.mNote: Short orchestral phrases come between the cello’s longer lines.

sections.label: C · Rapid figures and cantabile cello
sections.mNote: The soloist alternates rapid runs with broad phrases.

sections.label: D · Long solo for cello
sections.mNote: The late cello solo extends through pauses and changing tempos.

sections.label: E · cello, the concerto’s opening recitative
sections.mNote: The concerto’s opening recitative delays the final Allegro.

sections.label: Coda · Allegro in E minor
sections.mNote: The Allegro returns and closes in E minor.

cues.title: Cello recitative, opening of finale
cues.text: The orchestra opens the movement Allegro. The cello then enters, marked Moderato, quasi recitativo, with a solo in the manner of recitative, broken by pauses and chords and including a sudden run across the strings.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, opening of movement IV and rehearsals 42–43: orchestral Allegro, then Moderato, quasi recitativo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f6/IMSLP31083-PMLP14674-Elgar-Op085solo.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello entry, risoluto
cues.text: The cello takes up the finale’s brisk tune, marked risoluto (resolute). The solo phrases are accented, and the orchestra replies to each. Elgar breaks up the march with short rests.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, rehearsals 44–46: Allegro ma non troppo, risoluto, accented solo phrases and orchestral replies.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano at Brinkwells, 1918
cues.text: In August 1918 Elgar had an old Steinway upright brought to Brinkwells, his cottage in Sussex. He began the Violin Sonata the next day and went on to write the String Quartet and the Piano Quintet. The Cello Concerto followed in 1919.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Creating a Classic”, on the piano’s arrival and the sequence of chamber works and concerto: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Letter to Sidney Colvin, 1919
cues.text: In July 1919 Elgar told Sidney Colvin that he had nearly completed a cello concerto, “a real large work and I think good and alive”. He dedicated it to Sidney and Frances Colvin. On 8 August Alice posted the finished score from Fittleworth.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Sidney Colvin, late July 1919, quoted by Frank Beck; Alice’s posting of the score is dated 8 August in the same account: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: First performance, Queen’s Hall, 1919
cues.text: Felix Salmond gave the première at Queen’s Hall on 27 October 1919, with Elgar conducting. Albert Coates took most of the available rehearsal time for the rest of the programme, and the concerto was underprepared at its first performance.
cues.evidence: Première date and soloist: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Coates and the inadequate rehearsal: Adrian Jack’s BBC programme note, https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_celloconc.shtml

cues.title: Late solo passage, finale
cues.text: Late in the finale, at rehearsals 66–71 of the Novello solo-cello part, Elgar gave the cello an extended lament. It is marked Poco più lento, allargando and più tranquillo. Con passione appears over a phrase that contrasts with the orchestra’s earlier march.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 14, rehearsals 66–71: Poco più lento, allargando, con passione and più tranquillo. Frank Beck describes the late solo meditation: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final Allegro molto in E minor
cues.text: The finale’s theme returns, marked Allegro molto. Cello and orchestra exchange short, forceful phrases and close the concerto in E minor. The ending is brief and follows the long solo passage.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 14, rehearsals 73–74: Allegro molto and the E-minor close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
